title: Can You Trust What You Read? A Conversation About News and Critical Thinking

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: I saw something on my feed this morning — a news story that made me really angry. But then I started wondering whether it was actually true. I couldn't easily tell.

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: That happens to me all the time. What was it about?

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: It was about a politician supposedly saying something outrageous. But when I looked for the original quote, I couldn't find it anywhere except on one website I'd never heard of.

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: That's a classic sign. The first thing I always ask is: where is this story from? If it's from a site I've never heard of, or one that only ever publishes outrage-generating content, that tells me something.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: But isn't that a bit circular? You trust sources you already trust, and distrust ones you don't know. How do you actually verify something?

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: Good question. There are a few practical things. First: lateral reading. Instead of reading deeply into one source, you open multiple tabs and search for what other sources say about the same claim — especially what they say about the source itself.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: What do you mean by that?

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: If I come across an article from a site called, say, "TruePatriotNews," I don't just evaluate whether the article seems reasonable. I search for what others say about TruePatriotNews — whether it has a known bias, a track record of inaccuracy, whether it's been flagged by fact-checkers. The site itself might look professional, but its reputation might be very different.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: OK, that makes sense. What else?

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: Second: check whether the claim is being reported by multiple independent outlets. If a story is true and significant, reputable news organisations will typically cover it. If only one site is running it, that's a warning sign.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: What if there are multiple sites running it, but they're all citing each other?

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: That's a really important thing to notice. It's called a citation spiral — each site appears to be citing evidence, but they're all drawing from the same original source. You have to follow the chain back to the original claim. And often when you do, you find it's much weaker than it appeared.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: I've never heard the term "citation spiral" but I've definitely experienced it. And the emotional dimension — I noticed that the story made me angry, and I wonder whether that was by design.

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: Almost certainly. Emotional content spreads. If you notice that something is making you angry, or frightened, or outraged — that's a cue to pause. Not because your emotion is wrong, but because strong emotion can override critical thinking. The question to ask yourself is: "Is my anger based on verified facts, or on a story designed to make me feel this way?"

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: That's really useful. What about deepfakes — AI-generated videos? How do you tell those apart from real ones?

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: That's becoming much harder. For now, there are still technical signs — unnatural blinking, strange skin texture, slightly off audio sync. But the technology is improving fast. The honest answer is that this will become increasingly difficult, and it underlines why knowing whether a source is reliable matters more than ever — because the visual "evidence" can no longer be trusted on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Davyd
dialogue.text: It is. But the fundamentals haven't changed: ask where something comes from, who benefits from you believing it, and whether multiple credible sources confirm it. Those questions were useful before the internet, and they're still useful now.
